segments.text: The static has a texture. Not the flat white noise of a poorly grounded receiver.
This is something finer. Something with grain to it. The way the surface of old paper has grain
when you press it between two fingers and drag them slowly across. The headphones are heavy.
Not the polished consumer weight of something designed for comfort. The weight of iron and
bakelight and the wire mesh of a diaphragm built to work. Not to please. They press against the
skull at the temples and seal the ears completely and what they seal you into is not silence.
The ship is still out there. The engine is still turning. The hull is still pushing through water
at anchor. The small rocking motion of a large vessel in low Pacific swells. But the headphones
have reassigned all of that. Engine vibration. Water against the hull. The creak of the vessel's frame
responding to the pressure of its own weight. All of it reduced to a vibration that the body
receives through the soles of the feet. Through the seat of the chair. At a frequency below speech.
The headphones have given you something else instead. The central Pacific has electricity.
3,105 kHz. The frequency that has been open all night. The dial is set. The log sheet is on the
desk. And the pencil is resting in the hand. And the paper is slightly damp. Not wet. Not
uncomfortable. But damp in the way everything on a Coast Guard cutter in the Pacific is slightly
damp in the morning hours when the humidity has had all night to work. The pencil leaves marks
that are a fraction softer than they would be on dry paper. The marks are sharper this way somehow.
More decisive. The date in the log's upper margin. July 2nd, 1937. The time. 0415 local.
The entries so far are routine. A position check. A weather notation. The kind of entries that exist
in log books to prove that someone was paying attention. That the machinery was on. The watch
was held. The frequency was monitored. There is nothing yet on 3,105 kHz. The static breathes.
That is the only word for it. A trained ear hears the difference between dead static and a live
channel. The quality of the noise changes with atmospheric conditions. With the angle of the
signal paths across the Pacific on any given night. Right now the static is moving. Not words.
Not signal. But the texture of a channel that the ionosphere is carrying that has traveled
10,000 miles of atmospheric bounce already this morning and is still traveling. The static at
this frequency at this hour feels. And the word is not imprecise. Inhabited. Then. A voice.
Through the grain of the static. Through the 10,000 miles of atmospheric travel.
Through the Bakelite cups of the headphones pressed against your skull. A woman's voice.
She is reporting. She is calm. She's been doing this for hours. And the calm is not ease.
It is the composure of someone who has converted effort into discipline and has been running on
discipline long enough that it no longer costs what it cost at the beginning. She gives co-ordinate.
She gives an altitude. 1000 feet. She reports what she sees below her. Which is ocean.
And what she sees ahead of her. Which is ocean. And what she cannot see. Which is the island she
is looking for. The voice does not identify itself. The voice does not give a name. The voice gives
information. And the information it gives is the information of someone who needs to be found.
The pencil moves. The log sheet receives the entry. 0742.
H-A-Q-Q calling Itasca. We must be on you but cannot see you but gas is running low.
Been unable to reach you by radio. We are flying at 1000 feet.
Signal strength. S5. The strongest the equipment registers.
The strongest a signal gets. The needle pinned.
He stands up. The radio man stands up from the receiver desk in the radio room of the USCGC
Itasca. And the headphones come off his head in one motion. The cups pulling away from his ears.
And the ship comes back. All of it at once. The engines low continuous percussion.
The water working against the hull. The ventilation systems rush and hiss.
The sounds that the headphones had been keeping at bay for the past eight hours of watch are
suddenly present again. Not gradually but all at once as if someone has opened a door between
two rooms with different atmospheres. And the pressure has equalized instantly.
Leo Bellet's runs. Metal deck under foot. The ring of boot soles on the companion way of a
Coast Guard cutter. Not the dull thud of a wooden deck. Not the soft absorption of carpet.
But the ring of hard soles on painted steel. A sound that travels up through the legs.
And into the joints of anyone who has been running on ships for long enough to stop noticing it.
The stairs up to the bridge. Narrow. The angle steep. One hand on the rail.
Not for balance but out of the habit of ships. Through the hatchway. The bridge.
July 2nd 1937. The Central Pacific. The air on the open bridge of a cutter.
Is not the same air as the radio room. The radio room is sealed and heated by the equipment
and smells of warm electronics. And brass fittings and the accumulated exhalations
of men who have been awake for hours. The bridge is open. And the Pacific is right there.
Not the idea of the Pacific. But the fact of it. The air is salt and heat. And the thin chemical
smell of the Etasca's stack smoke. Bending in the wind above the vessel.
The smoke column. You can see it. Bending southeast. The signal fire they have been burning
to make a visible smoke marker. Black grey against the morning sky. Rising and bending.
He looks at the sky. The signal at S5 means close. Maximum signal strength at this frequency.
From this type of aircraft. From this type of transmitter. The range is 50 miles.
Maybe a hundred in ideal conditions. She is not across the Pacific from here. She is here.
She's close enough that the signal is pinning the needle. And she should be visible. Coming in
from the west southwest. The silver shape of the Lockheed Electra. Descending toward Howland Island.
The sky is empty. Not overcast. There are clouds. The morning cumulus of the equatorial Pacific.
Discrete and scattered. Not a ceiling. Between the clouds. Open sky. And in the open sky. No aircraft.
A horizon in every direction. Water. The smoke column from the Etasca's own stack.
The low profile of Howland Island to the east. Or what should be Howland Island?
Two miles of coral. Barely distinguishable from the surface of the sea. No aircraft.
The strongest signal his receiver has logged in eight hours of watch.
Is coming from a sky that contains nothing he can locate.
Leo Bellas stands on the bridge of the Etasca and looks at the empty sky.
The signal is still coming through on the frequency.
It was S5 when he left the radio room 30 seconds ago. It will be S5 when he goes back.
There is nothing in the sky. He will carry this moment for the rest of his life. Not the disappearance.
The moment before it. The sound of a voice at maximum strength.
The empty sky. The 40 year gap between those two facts.
In the days after July 2nd there were other reports.
Stations across the Pacific. And farther along the American coasts. Filed reception reports
on or near the frequency. Broken transmissions. Voice fragments.
Possible signals bearing toward the central Pacific.
The Navy had assumed control of the search. The reports came in.
They were assessed. They were filed. Atmospheric interference. Ionospheric skip. Unconfirmed.
The investigation notes this. It returns to it.
The woman's voice belongs to Amelia Earhart. This is not a secret. And has never been.
The call sign KHAQ identifies her aircraft. The Lockheed model. 10E Electra. Registration NR
1602O. A twin engine aluminum aircraft that she and her navigator have been flying across the Pacific
for the past 18 to 20 hours. The circumnavigation attempt. July 1937.
She was trying to fly around the world. It requires a moment. Not commentary but context.
To understand what that meant in 1937. The first solo non-stop transatlantic flight.
Had occurred 10 years earlier. Commercial passenger aviation was a decade old.
And still a luxury. The Pacific crossing by air was a technical achievement of recent vintage.
Pan American Airways had inaugurated its Trans Pacific Clipper service. Only two years prior.
The routes existed. The distances had been crossed. But they had been crossed with every
possible advantage. With full ground crews. With relay stations. With navigational aids along the
route. With the ability to land at intermediate points. Earhart was crossing the Pacific with
one navigator. One aircraft. And the radio on 3105. She had tried this once before.
In March of 1937. The same aircraft. The same route. A ground loop on takeoff in Honolulu.
Had ended the attempt before it began. The plane damaged. The crew unhurt. But the plan reset.
The second attempt began June 1st 1937. From Oakland. Heading east. Miami. Puerto Rico.
South America. Africa. India. Southeast Asia. Australia. New Guinea.
Leigh. New Guinea. The last stop before Howland Island. The leg from Leigh to Howland
is 2,243 nautical miles of open ocean. There is nothing between Leigh and Howland.
Not a landing strip. Not an airfield. Not a stretch of land large enough to set a twin
engine aircraft down. The Pacific. And then Howland Island. Less than a mile and a half long.
Half a mile wide. At its highest point 10 feet above sea level. The target for a navigation
shot from 2,000 miles out. On July 2nd 1937. At approximately 10 in the morning local time.
The Electra took off from Leigh. The takeoff was nearly the end. The Electra was loaded to maximum.
1,100 gallons of aviation fuel in tanks that run through the fuselage.
Inside the aircraft. Behind the firewall. In every cavity the designers had provisioned for them.
The aircraft's gross takeoff weight at this loading was at or near the limit
of what the airframe was certified for. The runway at Leigh ran to the harbour edge.
There was a grass strip. A slight downhill grade. And then the harbour.
And then the Pacific. When the Electra lifted off. It did not climb immediately. It descended.
The wheels left the ground and the aircraft sank toward the water. Heavy with fuel. And the physics
of a wing not yet generating sufficient lift at the speed it had achieved at the runway's end.
6 feet. The Electra descended to within 6 feet of the harbour surface. Before the airspeed
built enough for the wing to assert itself against the weight. 6 feet of clearance between the
landing gear and the Pacific Ocean. In the first 30 seconds of a 20 hour flight. Then it climbed.
Slowly. Settling into the altitude that would be its home for the next 18 hours.
1000 feet above the water. Low enough to stay below the high altitude overcast.
High enough to have some margin. Two Pratt and Whitney Wasp radial engines.
Each delivering 600 horsepower. Pushing the aircraft at a cruise speed of approximately
150 miles per hour. Across an ocean that offered no reference points and no forgiveness.
That is the aircraft. That is the pilot. The man in the back of the aircraft
is the one the popular account consistently forget. Frederick Yosef Nunin. Born April 4th,
1893 in Cook County, Illinois. 44 years old in the summer of 1937. He sits behind a wooden bulkhead
that divides the Electra's fuselage. The cockpit forward. The navigation space aft.
And he cannot see Earhart. And she cannot see him. Except through a small gap in the partition.
Communication happens by note. Passed forward through the gap. Or by shouting over two Pratt
and Whitney radials at cruise power. He was the most experienced Pacific Aerial Navigator alive.
This is not hyperbole. Pan-American Airways hired Nunin in 1930 to help chart the Trans-Pacific
Clipper routes. Midway, Wake Island, Guam, the Philippines, Hong Kong. He flew the survey missions.
He made the measurements. He established the waypoint positions that the Clipper service
would follow for the next decade. He knew the Pacific not from maps, but from the experience
of finding small islands in large oceans. Using the instruments available to a navigator in the 1930s.
A bubble sextant. A chronometer. A drift meter. And the sun. At the end of 1936. Pan-American let him go.
The company archive interviews site drinking. The precise circumstances are not reconstructed here.
What is established? Nunin was available when Earhart needed a navigator for the world flight.
He took the job. And on March 27, 1937. Two months and six days before the Electra disappeared.
He married Mary Beatrice Martinelli in Yuba City, California. Two months married.
He is sitting behind the bulkhead. His job is to tell Earhart where they are.
Which requires first determining where they are. Which in the open Pacific in 1937 means
taking a sun shot with the bubble sextant when the sun is visible. Running the celestial
mathematics to determine a line of position. Comparing that line to the dead reckoning track.
Adjusting the estimate. Doing this repeatedly every hour or two.
Across 18 hours of flight. Handing the result forward through the gap in the partition.
Earhart adjusting the heading accordingly. The procedure works when the sky is clear.
The sky has not been entirely clear. The Electra has been flying since 10 in the morning.
Lay time. It is now the early hours of July 2nd, 1937. Ship time aboard the Etasca.
Which means it is already July 2nd across the international date line. Which Earhart crossed
during the night. She has been in the air for what is now approximately 15 to 16 hours.
The engines have been running for 15 to 16 hours. The fuel load. 1100 gallons at departure
has been decreasing for 15 to 16 hours. The gauges on the instrument panel are showing
numbers that get worse as the flight continues. Close your eyes. Not a request. A necessity.
The radio room of the Etasca is gone. Belas is gone. The log is gone.
What remains is the interior of the Electra. And you are in it. The engines arrive first.
Not the sound of engines heard from outside. The sound of engines when you are inside the
aircraft they are attached to. Two Pratt and Whitney radials at cruise power produce a chord.
Not a single note. Not a roar. But a complex mechanical harmony that enters through every
surface simultaneously. Through the seat. Through the rudder pedals. Through the control column
under the hands. Through the soles of the shoes pressed against the floor. The engines are not
heard so much as they are absorbed. After 15 hours this frequency has become the frequency of the
world. The body has reorganized itself around it. The quiet at this point would be the shock.
The instrument panel glows. Dials in darkness. The altimeter reading 1000 feet. The air speed
indicator. 145 miles per hour. Slightly below crew. The aircraft running lean to preserve fuel.
The fuel gauges. The fuel gauges are the ones you return to. They are the ones that have been
drifting leftward since lay. The needles moving so slowly that any single observation reveals nothing.
But the trend across ours is clear. The tanks are draining. Below the aircraft. Nothing.
Not nothing in the way that the surface of a city at night is nothing. There are lights down there.
There is evidence of human presence. The planet announcing itself. Nothing in the way that the
Pacific announces itself. Darkness absolute and darkness. And the particular absence of any
feature that would tell a human eye where the water ends and the sky begins.
The stars have gone behind cloud. The horizon does not exist in any practical sense.
The artificial horizon on the instrument panel. The gyroscopic instrument that substitutes for
the absent real horizon is the only evidence the aircraft is level. You are in the most precisely
instrumented aircraft Amelia Earhart could obtain in the hands of the most experienced Pacific
navigator alive. And you are flying through the darkness that exists when there is nothing below
and nothing above. And nothing to either side except the Pacific which has no edges
and no markers and offers only this. A surface two thousand miles from where you started
that you cannot see from one thousand feet in the dark. A note comes through the gap in the
partition. Not a voice. Noonan communicates by note because the engines are too loud for
conversation through a wooden partition. His handwriting. And this matters. This is a specific
thing. Not a decoration. It's steady. 18 hours of turbulence and the vibration of two engines
and the cold at altitude have done nothing to the handwriting. The hand that produced the
celestial calculations on the charts in the navigation space aft has the quality of a hand
that has been trained to remain steady because unsteady hands produce numbers that end flights.
The note gives a sun line. A line of position calculated from the last sun shot.
Two numbers 157 degrees and 337 degrees. The aircraft is somewhere on that line.
The line runs through the Pacific like a thread. You are on the thread somewhere.
But the thread is long. And Howland Island is a bead on the thread the size of nothing.
The sun line is all he has. The time is approximately 0712. Itasca ship time.
Howland Island should be visible from one thousand feet if the clouds cooperate.
If the haze is not too thick. If the morning angle of the sun is not throwing the coral flat
into shadow that makes it vanish against the water. Two miles of island. 10 feet high
against the surface of a sea that has been coloured by overcast to a shade not meaningfully different
from coral at distance. The horizon is empty. Water. Cloud shadow on water. The smoke column
from the Itasca stack. Visible according to the plan from 20 miles or more. Which should be
directly ahead. Which should be resolving into a smudge on the horizon by now. Ahead. Water.
To the left. Water. To the right. Water. Behind the aircraft. To the west south west.
Leigh and New Guinea have been below the horizon for 17 hours. The fuel gauges.
The fuel gauges are the clocks in this aircraft. They are measuring the same passage of time
as the clock on the instrument panel. But in different units. Not hours and minutes.
But the irreversible mathematics of how long a Pratt and Whitney Wasp radial can run on what
remains in the tanks. The calculation does not get better. It runs in one direction.
It has been running in that direction for 17 hours. Howland Island is less than a
mile and a half long. 10 feet high. Invisible. July 2nd, 1937. The USCEC Itasca.
Anchored off the western shore of Howland Island. The radio log is open on the desk.
The entries begin accumulating in the morning hours. 0512. The Itasca transmitting on 3105
kilohertz. Sending Morse code on schedule. The pattern they have been maintaining for the past
several hours. 0615. Same. 0645. A new method. The Itasca's operator begins transmitting a long
dash on 3105 kilohertz. A steady tone the aircraft can use to take a bearing. A radio direction
finding aid that requires only that the aircraft's equipment can receive it. No acknowledgement.
No bearing request. No signal from KHAQQ. The Itasca operator transmits. The frequency receives what
the frequency always receives at this hour of the morning. Static. Inhabited static of a live
channel in the Pacific. 0742. The voice. S5. We must be on you but cannot see you but gas is
running low. The pencil moves. 0758. A second transmission. We are circling but cannot hear you.
Go ahead on 7500 either now or on the schedule time on half hour. She cannot hear them. The Itasca
has been transmitting on the frequency. The Itasca has been transmitting on schedule.
On the agreed frequency. At full power. The signal is going out. There is no
equipment failure in the log. The transmitters are operating. The frequency is clear.
She is transmitting at S5. The maximum signal strength the equipment registers.
She is close enough that the signal is pinning the needle. She is transmitting from somewhere
that cannot be more than a hundred miles away. And she cannot hear them. This is the asymmetry.
Not equipment failure. Something more specific than that. A channel that carries signal in one
direction and not the other. A frequency that works for transmission and not for reception.
She is loud. She is clear. She is saying she cannot hear the station that is hearing her perfectly.
The radio man on the Itasca is Leo Bellart. His name appears in the log's authentication.
He has been awake since before the watch began. He is listening to a woman's voice
at maximum signal strength. Telling him she cannot hear him. At 0800. A third transmission.
AHAQ calling Itasca. We received your signals but unable to get a minimum.
Please take bearing on us and answer 3105 with voice. She received their signals.
That is the first confirmation from her end that the Itasca's transmissions are reaching
the aircraft. Some of them. Some of the time. But she cannot get a minimum. Which means she
tried to take a directional bearing on the Itasca's signal and could not determine the direction.
The signal was present but too inconsistent for the direction finding equipment to lock.
She is asking the Itasca to answer her on 3105 kilohertz voice. So she can take a bearing on
voice transmission. The Itasca answers on 3105 voice. Full power. No response.
Radio man third class Thomas O'Hare on the Itasca's secondary receiver during this watch
later asked a question that his supervisor noted in an operational debrief.
He asked it not as a formal inquiry not as a challenge but as a man who had been listening
to a frequency for hours and could not account for what the frequency was doing. He said
why couldn't she hear me on 3105. The question has not been fully answered.
Then at 0843. The final transmission.
Kikiku to Itasca. We are on the line 157337. We will repeat message. We will repeat this on
6210 kilo cycles. Wait. Then. We are running north and south. Then. Nothing. The frequency at 08.
For three. 3105 kilohertz. As five signal.
And silence. Not the silence of a signal that has gotten progressively weaker.
The signal was at maximum strength in the last transmission. Not the silence of equipment failure.
The silence of a radio that simply stopped transmitting on this frequency.
Because she said she was switching. 62110 kilohertz.
That was the frequency she named before she stopped. She was going to repeat the message
on 6210. She was going to transmit there. The Itasca could not receive voice on 62110 kilohertz.
Their receivers covered the frequency. But the Itasca could not transmit voice on 6210.
Only Morse code. The ground equipment had been configured for 3105.
When she moved to 6210. The channel she moved to was one the Itasca could hear.
But could not answer in the mode she was using. She moved to a frequency they could not follow.
She has been gone for six hours already. When O'Hare asks his question.
She is not going to answer it. The static on the frequency has the quality that O'Hare will try.
Later. In a private account that no official record will contain. To describe.
Not the absence of a signal. The presence of a channel that should have a signal in it and doesn't.
He will write in the July 2nd entry of a diary kept in his seabag during the operation.
The static sounds different when you're waiting for someone. It has a shape.
The shape of the voice that should be in it. He is a 23 year old radio man on a coast guard
cutter in the central Pacific. He has been listening to radio static for four years.
He knows the difference between a dead channel and a live one. He knows the difference between
atmospheric noise and signal shaped absence. The frequency has the shape of the voice that should
be in it. He will monitor 3105 off shift on his personal equipment for the next two days.
On the early morning of July 4th 0300. The dead watch. The hours when ionospheric conditions
favor long distance propagation. He will hear something that does not resolve into words
but has the quality of a word trying to form. He will file a report. The duty officer will
log it as atmospheric skip. Oh hair writes in the July 4th entry. It was not skip. I have
been listening to skip for four years. Skip does not say words. The duty officer's log will
categorize the report. The search will go on. The search will find nothing. Here is what the
official record established about the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Frederick Noonan and why
it is the right place to begin before it is the wrong place to stop. The aircraft was heavy.
1100 gallons of fuel is a great deal of fuel but a Pratt and Whitney Wasp radial engine
at cruise power burns approximately 12 to 14 gallons per hour per engine. Two engines. 18 to
20 hours of flight time to Howland. The mathematics allow almost no margin.
With favorable winds the margin is sufficient. With headwinds and the weather on the final
leg from lay included winds that pushed against the aircraft's track. The margin narrows to hours.
Then to an hour. Then to minutes. She was at 1000 feet when she transmitted at 0742.
She had been airborne for approximately 19 hours. She could not see Howland Island.
She was circling. She said so at 0758. Circling over a position she believed was correct.
Looking for an island that was not appearing on the horizon. The fuel that remained for circling
was the fuel she was burning while circling. Every minute of the circle brought the gauges
closer to the position that ends flights. The ocean in that part of the Pacific is
approximately 4000 meters deep. Two and a half miles. Straight down. The official position.
The position of the United States Navy. Of the Coast Guard. Of every official inquiry that followed.
Is that Earhart ran out of fuel somewhere near Howland Island. Attempted to ditch the
aircraft in the water. And sank. The search that followed was the largest air sea search in American
history to that point. Nine ships. 66 aircraft. Approximately 250,000 square miles of ocean.
17 days. The USS Lexington alone contributed 62 aircraft to the effort. The estimated cost
exceeded four million dollars in 1937 money. They found nothing. Not wreckage. Not fuel slick.
Not emergency equipment. Not a trace of the aircraft or the two people inside it.
The ocean at that depth in that region does not return what it takes. A twin engine aluminum
aircraft at two and a half miles of depth is not a recoverable object with the technology
available in 1937. Or in the decades immediately following. The absence of wreckage does not prove
the wreckage is not there. It proves the wreckage is not findable. Leo Bellets believed this. For
decades he believed it. In a letter written in 1961 to Fred Garner. A journalist and researcher
who was investigating the disappearance. Bellets wrote that Earhart was
peacefully on the bottom of the sea. No farther than 100 miles from Howland. He based this on a
signal strength. S5 means close. If the signal was S5 she was close. If she was close the search
found nothing. She went down close. The ocean close to Howland is deep. The wreckage is there.
He carried this for the rest of his life. He also carried the radio log. He had kept it. Not
because the Navy asked him to. Not as part of any formal documentation requirement.
But because he recognized even in the immediate aftermath that what the log contained was
significant. The sequence of transmissions. The signal strengths. The asymmetry between
what the Etasca heard and what the aircraft heard. He preserved it. Decades later he donated it to
the National Archives. Where it is now held as part of the Leo G Bellets papers. Dated 1937
through 1971. Anyone who wants to read the last thing Amelia Earhart said to another human being
can read it there. The crash and sink theory is not a theory in the pejorative sense.
It is an assessment based on the available evidence. The fuel math. The empty sky.
The search that found nothing. And the testimony of a man who was as close to the event as any
living person. It is the conclusion a careful experienced man reached after a lifetime of
considering the evidence he had personally observed. And it cannot account for the signals.
In the days following July 2nd 1937. Monitoring stations across the Pacific
filed reception reports on the frequency. Pan American Airways maintained radio
listening stations across the Pacific as part of the infrastructure for its Clipper service.
Midway Wake Island Honolulu and others. These stations were staffed by trained radio operators
who knew the difference between atmospheric interference and voice. They filed reports.
Their logs indicate possible voice transmissions on or near the frequency in the days after the
disappearance. A 15 year old girl in St. Petersburg, Florida named Betty Clank was listening to her
family's shortwave radio. She had the dial on 3105. She heard a woman's voice and she wrote in her
notebook was not publicized for decades. It is now held by a research organization that has
been investigating the disappearance for 40 years. The notebook is legible. The entries are dated.
The content of what she wrote has been examined by researchers who note that details she recorded,
details she would have had no knowledge of in 1937, are consistent with the known
circumstances of the flight. The Navy assessed the reports that came in during the search.
Atmospheric interference. Ionospheric skip. Unconfirmed. If the aircraft had gone down
in deep water and sunk, those assessments are correct. A radio that is two and a half miles
under water does not transmit. Atmospheric skip and interference account for what was heard.
The physics are clear. The physics are also clear in the other direction.
If the aircraft was not on the ocean floor, if it was on land, on a reef, on a beach,
a functional radio could transmit for days. The Electra's radio drew power from the aircraft's
batteries. The batteries would last while the batteries lasted. The fuel in the tanks was
not the fuel in the batteries. A landed aircraft, intact, with a functional radio and a pilot who
knew how to operate it, could put a signal on three 105 for days. 57 credible reception reports
were logged in the days after July 2nd. Credible in the sense that they came from trained operators
at stations with equipment capable of distinguishing voice from interference.
In some cases with directional bearings pointing towards the Central Pacific.
Pan-American Airways Chief Communications Officer in San Francisco
sent a routing memo to the Pacific Station managers on July 5th, 1937.
The memo instructed all Pacific stations to discontinue monitoring 3,105 kilohertz
effective immediately. Reception reports from the prior 72 hours were to be filed as
unconfirmed atmospheric phenomena. The memo noted that the Navy had assumed control of the search
and that continued monitoring at company expense was not operationally justified.
The stated reason is adequate and logical. A corporation does not continue expensive
monitoring operations after the responsible government agency has assumed control of the
relevant search. The memo reads, discontinue monitoring. File as unconfirmed atmospheric
phenomena. They were told to stop listening. Someone was still transmitting from somewhere.
The crash and sink theory does not get smaller when the post-loss signals arrive.
It gets insufficient. There is a difference. A theory that fails to explain an important fact
has not been disproved. It may still be correct. It may be that the signals were atmospheric.
It may be that 57 trained operators were all wrong in the same direction at the same time.
The theory remains. But the signals do not go away. They have been filed.
They have been assessed. They have been attributed to atmospheric phenomena
and moved to the appropriate category. They are still there, in the record, in the logs of
train radio operators at stations spread across the Pacific. A woman's voice on the frequency
in the days after the silence. Saying something. The line runs 157 degrees.
It runs 337 degrees in the other direction. A sun line. A line of position calculated from
a celestial observation. The result of Noonan's last reliable shot of the sun through the bubble
sextant before the clouds moved in and the horizon dissolved into haze. A sun line tells
a navigator's one thing. You are somewhere on this line. It does not say where on the line.
It says the line is the boundary of what can be known. You are on this side of uncertainty.
Beyond this, the mathematics stop. He passed it forward through the gap in the partition.
The numbers on paper in his steady hand. 157. 337.
Airheart reported them on the radio. They were the last coordinates she gave.
What a sun line means, no visionally, is this. If you know you are on the line,
and you know the line runs north, northwest, to south, southeast, and you know you are somewhere
near Howland Island, then you run the line. You fly it. You go north along 337 degrees
until the island appears. Or you go south along 157 degrees until the island appears.
Or you circle the intersection point and wait. She said she was running north and south.
She was flying the line. The line runs north, northwest through Howland Island.
Extended in that direction, it goes toward the Marshall Islands, toward Japan,
toward the broader Northern Pacific. Extended southeast, along the 157 degrees,
the line goes somewhere else. Approximately 400 miles south southeast of Howland Island,
along that bearing, is an island. The island was called Gardner Island on the charts of 1937.
It is now called Nicumororo. It sits at the southern end of the Phoenix Islands group,
approximately four and a half degrees south latitude, 174 degrees west longitude.
It is Coral Atoll, a ring of reef enclosing a central lagoon, with a land area of
approximately four and a half square miles. The terrain is low and flat. The interior is dense
with buka and rentries. The surrounding reef flat extends for several hundred meters at low tide.
